# What is the poverty rate in Anderson County,TN?
Updated May 28, 2026 Refreshed monthly
In 2020–2024, about 13.4% of the population lived under the poverty line.  The poverty rate is the percentage of people in a population whose household income falls below the poverty threshold set by the government. It measures the share of individuals or families who do not earn enough to meet basic needs such as food, housing, and healthcare. On average, 10,400 people were considered in poverty.

Poverty doesn’t affect all groups equally. Rates vary widely by demographic group, family type and location.
From 2015–2019 to 2020–2024, the poverty rate for children under 18 in Anderson County decreased from 22.2% to 16.7%. During the same period, the poverty rate for adults under 65 years decreased from 16.9% to 12.3%. For those older than 65, the poverty rate increased from 10.3% to 12.9%.

Among racial or ethnic groups in Anderson County during 2020–2024, three had a higher poverty rate than the county’s overall rate: Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino origin (of any race), and Two or more races.
Five groups had a lower than average poverty rate: American Indian and Alaska Native, Asian, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander, Some other race, and White alone, not Hispanic or Latino.
The poverty rate for the American Indian and Alaska Native population shifted the most, decreasing from 68.4% in 2015–2019 to 12.9% in 2020–2024.

## Notes
#### Notes:
The percentage of population below the poverty level comes from American Community Survey (ACS) variable S1701_C03_001E in table S1701.
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010-2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011-2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

It measures the share of individuals or families who do not earn enough to meet basic needs such as food, housing, and healthcare. On average, 10,400 people were considered in poverty.

## In 2020–2024, about 10,400 people in Anderson County, TN were living under the poverty line.
People living under poverty line
Source: US Census Bureau
In 2020–2024, about 10,400 people in Anderson County, TN were living under the poverty line.

Poverty doesn’t affect all groups equally. Rates vary widely by demographic group, family type and location.
From 2015–2019 to 2020–2024, the poverty rate for children under 18 in Anderson County decreased from 22.2% to 16.7%. During the same period, the poverty rate for adults under 65 years decreased from 16.9% to 12.3%. For those older than 65, the poverty rate increased from 10.3% to 12.9%.

#
## Notes
#### Notes:
The percentage of population below the poverty level comes from American Community Survey (ACS) variable S1701_C03_001E in table S1701.
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010-2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011-2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

In 2020–2024, about 13.4% of the population lived under the poverty line.  The poverty rate is the percentage of people in a population whose household income falls below the poverty threshold set by the government. It measures the share of individuals or families who do not earn enough to meet basic needs such as food, housing, and healthcare. On average, 10,400 people were considered in poverty.

Poverty doesn’t affect all groups equally. Rates vary widely by demographic group, family type and location.
From 2015–2019 to 2020–2024, the poverty rate for children under 18 in Anderson County decreased from 22.2% to 16.7%. During the same period, the poverty rate for adults under 65 years decreased from 16.9% to 12.3%. For those older than 65, the poverty rate increased from 10.3% to 12.9%.

Among racial or ethnic groups in Anderson County during 2020–2024, three had a higher poverty rate than the county’s overall rate: Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino origin (of any race), and Two or more races.
Five groups had a lower than average poverty rate: American Indian and Alaska Native, Asian, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander, Some other race, and White alone, not Hispanic or Latino.
The poverty rate for the American Indian and Alaska Native population shifted the most, decreasing from 68.4% in 2015–2019 to 12.9% in 2020–2024.

## Notes
#### Notes:
The percentage of population below the poverty level comes from American Community Survey (ACS) variable S1701_C03_001E in table S1701.
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010-2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011-2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

# What is the poverty rate in Anderson County,TN?
Updated May 28, 2026 Refreshed monthly
In 2020–2024, about 13.4% of the population lived under the poverty line.  The poverty rate is the percentage of people in a population whose household income falls below the poverty threshold set by the government. It measures the share of individuals or families who do not earn enough to meet basic needs such as food, housing, and healthcare. On average, 10,400 people were considered in poverty.

Based on data from the American Community Survey, Anderson County's poverty rate during 2020–2024 was lower than the 16.7% poverty rate during the previous five years (2015–2019).

## In 2020–2024, about 10,400 people in Anderson County, TN were living under the poverty line.
People living under poverty line

In 2020–2024, about 10,400 people in Anderson County, TN were living under the poverty line.

Poverty doesn’t affect all groups equally. Rates vary widely by demographic group, family type and location.
From 2015–2019 to 2020–2024, the poverty rate for children under 18 in Anderson County decreased from 22.2% to 16.7%. During the same period, the poverty rate for adults under 65 years decreased from 16.9% to 12.3%. For those older than 65, the poverty rate increased from 10.3% to 12.9%.

#
## Notes
#### Notes:
The percentage of population below the poverty level comes from American Community Survey (ACS) variable S1701_C03_001E in table S1701.
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010-2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011-2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

**Release:**Mean Commute Time
**Units:** Minutes,Not Seasonally Adjusted
**Frequency:** Annual

#
## Notes
#### Notes:
Mean commuting time is calculated by dividing the aggregate travel time to work for all workers (in minutes) by the total number of workers, 16-years old and older, who commute (ACS 5-year variables B08013_001E from table B08013 and B08012_001E from table B08012, respectively).
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010–2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011–2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

texts.10:
#
## Notes
#### Notes:
Mean commuting time is calculated by dividing the aggregate travel time to work for all workers (in minutes) by the total number of workers, 16-years old and older, who commute (ACS 5-year variables B08013_001E from table B08013 and B08012_001E from table B08012, respectively).
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010–2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011–2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

2016-2020 ACS 5-Year estimates of socioeconomic characteristics compiled at the County level. These characteristics include Aggregate Travel Time To Work Of Workers By Sex, Travel Time To Work, Poverty Status In The Past 12 Months Of Families By Household Type By Tenure, Poverty Status Of Individuals In The Past 12 Months By Living Arrangement, Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Median Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Aggregate Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Median Family Income In The Past 12 Months, Median Non-family Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Sex By Age By Employment Status For The Population 16 Years And Over, Tenure By Occupants Per Room, Total Population in Occupied Housing Units by Tenure by year Householder Moved into Unit, Tenure By Housing Costs As A Percentage Of Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Sex By Occupation For The Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over, Median Earnings In the Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) by Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over, Educational Attainment by Employment Status for the Population 25 to 64 Years, and Occupation By Median Earnings In The Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) For The Full-Time, Year-Round Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over.

The American Community Survey (ACS) 5 Year 2016-2020 socioeconomic estimate data is a subset of information derived from the following census tables: B08013 - Aggregate Travel Time To Work Of Workers By Sex; B08303 - Travel Time To Work; B17019 - Poverty Status In The Past 12 Months Of Families By Household Type By Tenure; B17021 - Poverty Status Of Individuals In The Past 12 Months By Living Arrangement; B19001 - Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B19013 - Median Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B19025 - Aggregate Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B19113 - Median Family Income In The Past 12 Months; B19202 - Median Non-family Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B23001 - Sex By Age By Employment Status For The Population 16 Years And Over; B25014 - Tenure By Occupants Per Room; B25026 - Total Population in Occupied Housing Units by Tenure by year Householder Moved into Unit; B25106 - Tenure By Housing Costs As A Percentage Of Household Income In The Past 12 Months; C24010 - Sex By Occupation For The Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over; B20004 - Median Earnings In the Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) by Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over; B23006 - Educational Attainment by Employment Status for the Population 25 to 64 Years, and; B24021 - Occupation By Median Earnings In The Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) For The Full-Time, Year-Round Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over. To learn more about the American Community Survey (ACS), and associated datasets visit: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs, for questions about the spatial attribution of this dataset, please reach out to us at GISHelpdesk@hud.gov.

2016-2020 ACS 5-Year estimates of socioeconomic characteristics compiled at the County level. These characteristics include Aggregate Travel Time To Work Of Workers By Sex, Travel Time To Work, Poverty Status In The Past 12 Months Of Families By Household Type By Tenure, Poverty Status Of Individuals In The Past 12 Months By Living Arrangement, Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Median Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Aggregate Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Median Family Income In The Past 12 Months, Median Non-family Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Sex By Age By Employment Status For The Population 16 Years And Over, Tenure By Occupants Per Room, Total Population in Occupied Housing Units by Tenure by year Householder Moved into Unit, Tenure By Housing Costs As A Percentage Of Household Income In The Past 12 Months, Sex By Occupation For The Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over, Median Earnings In the Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) by Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over, Educational Attainment by Employment Status for the Population 25 to 64 Years, and Occupation By Median Earnings In The Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) For The Full-Time, Year-Round Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over.
texts.1: The American Community Survey (ACS) 5 Year 2016-2020 socioeconomic estimate data is a subset of information derived from the following census tables: B08013 - Aggregate Travel Time To Work Of Workers By Sex; B08303 - Travel Time To Work; B17019 - Poverty Status In The Past 12 Months Of Families By Household Type By Tenure; B17021 - Poverty Status Of Individuals In The Past 12 Months By Living Arrangement; B19001 - Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B19013 - Median Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B19025 - Aggregate Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B19113 - Median Family Income In The Past 12 Months; B19202 - Median Non-family Household Income In The Past 12 Months; B23001 - Sex By Age By Employment Status For The Population 16 Years And Over; B25014 - Tenure By Occupants Per Room; B25026 - Total Population in Occupied Housing Units by Tenure by year Householder Moved into Unit; B25106 - Tenure By Housing Costs As A Percentage Of Household Income In The Past 12 Months; C24010 - Sex By Occupation For The Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over; B20004 - Median Earnings In the Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) by Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over; B23006 - Educational Attainment by Employment Status for the Population 25 to 64 Years, and; B24021 - Occupation By Median Earnings In The Past 12 Months (In 2015 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars) For The Full-Time, Year-Round Civilian Employed Population 16 Years And Over. ## Source
### Technical Note
The U.S. Census Bureau calculates 90% confidence intervals for American Community Survey estimates. Use caution when interpreting values with wide confidence intervals. Confidence intervals that are farther away from estimates in either direction indicate uncertainty due to small survey sample sizes. The U.S. Census Bureau does not recommend comparing overlapping 5-year periods since much of the data in each estimate are the same. Use caution when comparing estimates for census tracts over time as these geographies are redefined with each decennial census according to population changes.

Title: Selected Variables From the 2020
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
## Selected Variables From the 2020 - 2024 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates
CSV and GeoJSON files are available for states, counties, census tracts, and core-based statistical areas (CBSA).
Variable names for the data profile table variables are followed by USCB API variable names.
R code for generating these files using the USCB API
US Census Bureau (USCB). 2026. "2020 - 2024 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates." Released 29 January. https://data.census.gov.

## Geography
Polygons are from the USCB TIGER/Line cartographic boundary files.
*   GEOIDFQ: Fully-qualified GEOID code composed of a prefix and FIPS code that can be used to unambiguously join with US Census Bureau data from data.census.gov.  
*   ST (STUSPS): USPS two-letter state code (states, counties, and tracts only)  
*   Name (NAME): State name / county name / tract name / CBSA name  
*   Latitude: WGS 1984 latitude of the centroid calculated from the area polygons with st_centroid()  
*   Longitude: WGS 1984 longitude of the centroid calculated from the area polygons with st_centroid()  
*   Square_Miles: Land area in square miles calculated by dividing ALAND + AWATER (square meters) by 2,589,988

## Table DP02 - Selected Social Characteristics in the United States
*   Total_Households (DP02_0001E): Total number of households  
*   Average_Household_Size (DP02_0016E): Average number of persons per household  
*   Percent_Single_Mothers (DP02_0038PE): Percent of women 15 to 50 years old who had a birth in the past 12 months who were widowed, divorced, or never married  
*   Percent_In_College (DP02_0058PE): Percent of population 3 years or older enrolled in college or graduate school  
*   Percent_Bachelors_Degree (DP02_0065PE): Percent of population 25 years or older with a bachelor's degree  
*   Percent_Graduate_Degree (DP02_0066PE): Percent of population 25 years or older with a graduate or professional degree  
*   Percent_Veterans (DP02_0070PE): Percent of population over 18 years of age that are civilian veterans of the armed forces  
*   Percent_Disabled (DP02_0072PE): percent of the total civilian noninstitutionalized population with a disability. Disability types include hearing difficulty, vision difficulty, cognitive difficulty, ambulatory difficulty, self-care difficulty, and independent living difficulty  
*   Percent_Foreign_Born (DP02_0094PE): Percent of population born outside the USA

## Table DP03 - Selected Economic Characteristics
*   Workforce_Participation (DP03_0002PE): Percent of population 16 years and over in the labor force  
*   Percent_Unemployed (DP03_0009PE): Percent of civillian labor force unemployed. Note that this is a value captured in the survey period that may not accurately reflect either current or long-term structural conditions  
*   Percent_Commute_Alone (DP03_0019PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that drive to work alone in a car, truck, or van  
*   Percent_Commute_Transit (DP03_0021PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that commute to work by public transportation, exclusing taxicabs  
*   Percent_Commute_Walk (DP03_0022PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that commute to work by walking  
*   Percent_Work_at_Home (DP03_0024PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that commute to work at home  
*   Mean_Commute_Minutes (DP03_0025E): Mean travel time to work in minutes for workers 16 years of age and older  
*   Percent_Jobs_Management (DP03_0027PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in management, business, science, and arts occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Service (DP03_0028PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in service occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Sales (DP03_0029PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in sales and office occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Nat_Resources (DP03_0030PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in natural resources, construction, and maintenance occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Production (DP03_0031PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in production, transportation, and material moving occupations  
*   Percent_Industry_Ag_Mining (DP03_0033PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, and mining  

## Table DP03 - Selected Economic Characteristics
*   Percent_Industry_Construction (DP03_0034PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in construction  
*   Percent_Industry_Manufacturing (DP03_0035PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in manufacturing  
*   Percent_Industry_Wholesale (DP03_0036PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in wholesale trade  
*   Percent_Industry_Retail (DP03_0037PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in retail trade  
*   Percent_Industry_Transport (DP03_0038PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in transportation and warehousing, and utilities  
*   Percent_Industry_Information (DP03_0039PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in information  
*   Percent_Industry_Finance (DP03_0040PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in finance and insurance, and real estate and rental and leasing  
*   Percent_Industry_Pro_Services (DP03_0041PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in professional, scientific, and management, and administrative and waste management services  
*   Percent_Industry_Education (DP03_0042PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in educational services, and health care and social assistance  
*   Percent_Industry_Recreation (DP03_0043PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in arts, entertainment, and recreation, and accommodation and food services  
*   Percent_Private_Employed (DP03_0047PE): Percent civilian employed population 16 years and over as private wage and salary workers  
*   Percent_Govt_Employed (DP03_0048PE): Percent civilian employed population 16 years and over as government workers  
*   Percent_Self_Employed (DP03_0049PE): Percent civilian employed population 16 years and over that are self-employed in own not incorporated business workers  

## Table DP03 - Selected Economic Characteristics
*   Median_Household_Income (DP03_0062E): Median household income and benefits in 2023 inflation-adjusted dollars  
*   Percent_Health_Insurance (DP03_0096PE): Percent of the civilian noninstitutionalized population with health insurance coverage

## Table DP04 - Selected Housing Characteristics
*   Total_Housing_Units (DP04_0001E): Total housing units  
*   Percent_Vacant_Units (DP04_0003PE): Percent vacant housing units  
*   Percent_2020_2024_Units (DP04_0017PE): Percent of housing units built 2020-2024  
*   Percent_2010_2019_Units (DP04_0018PE): Percent of housing units built 2010-2019  
*   Percent_Pre_War_Units (DP04_0026PE): Percent of housing units built in 1939 or earlier  
*   Homeownership_Percent (DP04_0046PE): Percent of occupied housing units occupied by the owner  
*   Percent_Renters (DP04_0047PE): Percent of housing units occupied by a renter  
*   Percent_No_Vehicle (DP04_0058PE): Percent of occupied housing units where no vehicle is available  
*   Median_Home_Value (DP04_0089E): Median value of owner-occupied housing units  
*   Median_Monthly_Mortgage (DP04_0101E): Median selected monthly owner costs in dollars for housing units with a mortgage  
*   Median_Monthly_Rent (DP04_0134E): Median monthly rent in dollars for occupied housing units paying rent  
*   Percent_Unaffordable_Rent (DP04_0142PE): Percent of occupied units paying rent that is 35% or more of household income

## Table DP05 - Demographic and Housing Estimates
*   Total_Population (DP05_0001E): Total population  
*   Median_Age (DP05_0018E): Median age in years  
*   Percent_Under_5 (DP05_0005PE): Percent of total population under five years of age  
*   Percent_Under_18 (DP05_0019PE): Percent of total population under 18 years of age  
*   Percent_Over_64 (DP05_0024PE): Percent of total population 65 years of age or older  
*   Pop_per_Square_Mile: Total_Population divided by Square_Miles

## Selected Variables From the 2020 - 2024 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates
CSV and GeoJSON files are available for states, counties, census tracts, and core-based statistical areas (CBSA).
Variable names for the data profile table variables are followed by USCB API variable names.
R code for generating these files using the USCB API
US Census Bureau (USCB). 2026. "2020 - 2024 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates." Released 29 January. https://data.census.gov.
texts.1:
## Geography
Polygons are from the USCB TIGER/Line cartographic boundary files.
*   GEOIDFQ: Fully-qualified GEOID code composed of a prefix and FIPS code that can be used to unambiguously join with US Census Bureau data from data.census.gov.  
*   ST (STUSPS): USPS two-letter state code (states, counties, and tracts only)  
*   Name (NAME): State name / county name / tract name / CBSA name  
*   Latitude: WGS 1984 latitude of the centroid calculated from the area polygons with st_centroid()  
*   Longitude: WGS 1984 longitude of the centroid calculated from the area polygons with st_centroid()  
*   Square_Miles: Land area in square miles calculated by dividing ALAND + AWATER (square meters) by 2,589,988
texts.2:
## Table DP02 - Selected Social Characteristics in the United States
*   Total_Households (DP02_0001E): Total number of households  
*   Average_Household_Size (DP02_0016E): Average number of persons per household  
*   Percent_Single_Mothers (DP02_0038PE): Percent of women 15 to 50 years old who had a birth in the past 12 months who were widowed, divorced, or never married  
*   Percent_In_College (DP02_0058PE): Percent of population 3 years or older enrolled in college or graduate school  
*   Percent_Bachelors_Degree (DP02_0065PE): Percent of population 25 years or older with a bachelor's degree  
*   Percent_Graduate_Degree (DP02_0066PE): Percent of population 25 years or older with a graduate or professional degree  
*   Percent_Veterans (DP02_0070PE): Percent of population over 18 years of age that are civilian veterans of the armed forces  
*   Percent_Disabled (DP02_0072PE): percent of the total civilian noninstitutionalized population with a disability. Disability types include hearing difficulty, vision difficulty, cognitive difficulty, ambulatory difficulty, self-care difficulty, and independent living difficulty  
*   Percent_Foreign_Born (DP02_0094PE): Percent of population born outside the USA
texts.3:
## Table DP03 - Selected Economic Characteristics
*   Workforce_Participation (DP03_0002PE): Percent of population 16 years and over in the labor force  
*   Percent_Unemployed (DP03_0009PE): Percent of civillian labor force unemployed. Note that this is a value captured in the survey period that may not accurately reflect either current or long-term structural conditions  
*   Percent_Commute_Alone (DP03_0019PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that drive to work alone in a car, truck, or van  
*   Percent_Commute_Transit (DP03_0021PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that commute to work by public transportation, exclusing taxicabs  
*   Percent_Commute_Walk (DP03_0022PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that commute to work by walking  
*   Percent_Work_at_Home (DP03_0024PE): Percent of workers 16 years or over that commute to work at home  
*   Mean_Commute_Minutes (DP03_0025E): Mean travel time to work in minutes for workers 16 years of age and older  
*   Percent_Jobs_Management (DP03_0027PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in management, business, science, and arts occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Service (DP03_0028PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in service occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Sales (DP03_0029PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in sales and office occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Nat_Resources (DP03_0030PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in natural resources, construction, and maintenance occupations  
*   Percent_Jobs_Production (DP03_0031PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over in production, transportation, and material moving occupations  
*   Percent_Industry_Ag_Mining (DP03_0033PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting, and mining
texts.4:
## Table DP03 - Selected Economic Characteristics
*   Percent_Industry_Construction (DP03_0034PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in construction  
*   Percent_Industry_Manufacturing (DP03_0035PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in manufacturing  
*   Percent_Industry_Wholesale (DP03_0036PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in wholesale trade  
*   Percent_Industry_Retail (DP03_0037PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in retail trade  
*   Percent_Industry_Transport (DP03_0038PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in transportation and warehousing, and utilities  
*   Percent_Industry_Information (DP03_0039PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in information  
*   Percent_Industry_Finance (DP03_0040PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in finance and insurance, and real estate and rental and leasing  
*   Percent_Industry_Pro_Services (DP03_0041PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in professional, scientific, and management, and administrative and waste management services  
*   Percent_Industry_Education (DP03_0042PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in educational services, and health care and social assistance  
*   Percent_Industry_Recreation (DP03_0043PE): Percent of civillian employed population 16 years or over working in arts, entertainment, and recreation, and accommodation and food services  
*   Percent_Private_Employed (DP03_0047PE): Percent civilian employed population 16 years and over as private wage and salary workers  
*   Percent_Govt_Employed (DP03_0048PE): Percent civilian employed population 16 years and over as government workers  
*   Percent_Self_Employed (DP03_0049PE): Percent civilian employed population 16 years and over that are self-employed in own not incorporated business workers
texts.5:
## Table DP03 - Selected Economic Characteristics
*   Median_Household_Income (DP03_0062E): Median household income and benefits in 2023 inflation-adjusted dollars  
*   Percent_Health_Insurance (DP03_0096PE): Percent of the civilian noninstitutionalized population with health insurance coverage
texts.6:
## Table DP04 - Selected Housing Characteristics
*   Total_Housing_Units (DP04_0001E): Total housing units  
*   Percent_Vacant_Units (DP04_0003PE): Percent vacant housing units  
*   Percent_2020_2024_Units (DP04_0017PE): Percent of housing units built 2020-2024  
*   Percent_2010_2019_Units (DP04_0018PE): Percent of housing units built 2010-2019  
*   Percent_Pre_War_Units (DP04_0026PE): Percent of housing units built in 1939 or earlier  
*   Homeownership_Percent (DP04_0046PE): Percent of occupied housing units occupied by the owner  
*   Percent_Renters (DP04_0047PE): Percent of housing units occupied by a renter  
*   Percent_No_Vehicle (DP04_0058PE): Percent of occupied housing units where no vehicle is available  
*   Median_Home_Value (DP04_0089E): Median value of owner-occupied housing units  
*   Median_Monthly_Mortgage (DP04_0101E): Median selected monthly owner costs in dollars for housing units with a mortgage  
*   Median_Monthly_Rent (DP04_0134E): Median monthly rent in dollars for occupied housing units paying rent  
*   Percent_Unaffordable_Rent (DP04_0142PE): Percent of occupied units paying rent that is 35% or more of household income
texts.7:
## Table DP05 - Demographic and Housing Estimates
*   Total_Population (DP05_0001E): Total population  
*   Median_Age (DP05_0018E): Median age in years  
*   Percent_Under_5 (DP05_0005PE): Percent of total population under five years of age  
*   Percent_Under_18 (DP05_0019PE): Percent of total population under 18 years of age  
*   Percent_Over_64 (DP05_0024PE): Percent of total population 65 years of age or older  
*   Pop_per_Square_Mile: Total_Population divided by Square_Miles

# Older Drivers at Work
For Everyone
Oct. 28, 2026, visit link for details.

# Older Drivers at Work
## Key points
People 55 years and older are a growing group of the U.S. population that continues to work and drive. While older workers are more likely to adopt safe driving behaviors, they are also at greater risk of serious injury if they are involved in a crash. Employers can take actions to keep older drivers safe on the job.

# Older Drivers at Work
## Why it's important
Older workers (those ages 55 and older) bring extensive skills, knowledge, and experience built over the course of a lifespan. However, age-related physical and mental changes may affect older workers’ driving. While such changes are normal, they also put older drivers at a greater risk of dying if they are in a motor vehicle crash. Employers and workers share the responsibility for keeping older drivers safe at work.

# Older Drivers at Work
## Facts and stats
*   By 2030, 32% of the U.S. population is expected to be age 55 or older, an increase from 30% in 2022. The share that is age 65 or older will grow even more: from 17% in 2022 to 21% in 2030.1  
*   Over the 2016-2026 period, workers ages 75 and older are expected to have the fastest rate of growth in the labor force (91.5%), followed by workers 65 to 74 years (50.3%).2  
*   By 2030, 85% to 90% of Americans age 65 or older will be licensed to drive.3  
*   Research shows that older drivers are more likely than their younger counterparts to adopt safe behaviors such as wearing a seat belt and complying with speed limits. However, those age 55 and older have twice the risk of dying in a work-related crash than younger workers do.4 It is normal for physical and mental abilities to decline with age – putting older workers at greater risk of serious injury if they are involved in a motor vehicle crash.  
*   In 2022 motor vehicle crashes accounted for 36% of all work-related deaths among workers age 55 or older.5

# Older Drivers at Work
## What employers can do
Use the following recommendations to develop safety and health programs that consider older drivers' needs.
*   Consider whether the work can be done without driving. Reducing the amount of driving workers do is the most effective way to prevent motor vehicle crashes.  
*   Set policies that allow drivers to consult with their supervisors to adjust driving hours if they have trouble seeing at night, and to stop driving if they are too tired or the weather is bad.  
*   Provide refresher driving training that includes topics such as safe-driving strategies, changes in road rules, regulations on distracted driving, and new vehicle safety features.  
*   Restrict driving based on assessment of actual driving ability, rather than general health status or an arbitrary age limit.  
*   Give workers general information about the possible effects of prescription and over-the-counter medications on their driving.

# Older Drivers at Work
## What workers can do
If you are an older worker driving as part of your job:
*   Talk with your doctor or pharmacist about potential effects of your medications on safe driving.  
*   Get a thorough eye exam at least every 1-2 years, as your vision may change with age.  
*   Maintain good health by engaging in regular physical activity, eating a healthy diet, getting enough sleep, and complying with all health exams and screenings.  
*   Use a driving self-assessment tool to evaluate your driving.  
*   Talk with your supervisor if you are having difficulty with driving, as you may need to change your driving habits.

# Older Drivers
## Overview
In 2021 more than 20% of licensed drivers in the United States were 65 or older (FHWA, 2022). As drivers age, their physical and mental abilities, driving behaviors, and crash risks all change, though age alone does not determine driving performance. Many features of the current system of roads, traffic signals and controls, laws, licensing practices, and vehicles were not designed to accommodate older drivers. Older Americans are increasingly dependent on driving to maintain their mobility, independence, and health. The challenge is to balance mobility for older drivers with safety for all road users.
The U.S. population 65 and older increased at a much faster rate (35.1%) than the total population (7.4%) from the years 2010 to 2020 (U.S. Census Bureau, 2010, 2020). The U.S. Census Bureau estimates that by 2030 the resident population over 65 will be 73 million and will comprise 21% of the total U.S. population (Vespa et al., 2020).
As the U.S. population 65 and older has grown, the proportion of licensed drivers 65+ has also risen, from 14% in 2001 to 21% in 2021 (FHWA, 2002, 2022). The proportion of fatal crashes involving older drivers follows a similar trend, rising from 11% in 2001 to 19% in 2021.

The number of fatalities involving older drivers has been increasing in recent years, after experiencing a period of decline from 2000 to 2009. In 2021 there were 8,209 fatalities involving older drivers compared to the 29-year low of 5,613 in 2009 (NCSA, 2012; NHTSA, 2023). However, the older population has grown at a rate faster than the increase in fatalities involving older drivers.

# Older Drivers
## Overview
Not only is the U.S. population aging, with older people making up a larger proportion of the total population, but drivers are maintaining their licenses for longer as well. The proportion of people 65 or older who held driver licenses rose from 78% in 2001 to 89% in 2021 (FHWA, 2002,2022b; U.S. Census Bureau 2011, 2022). Notably, 59% of people 85 years and older maintained their licenses in 2020, compared to approximately half (50%) who maintained licenses in 2000 (FHWA, 2002, 2022b).
With current life expectancy in this country at 78.8 years on average (Kochaneck et al., 2020), and with advances in medical science, older Americans are staying mobile and active longer. Those who will reach 65 in the coming decade have been projected to drive more miles and are expected to continue driving later in life than previous generations. This increasingly active and mobile older population gives rise to the need to enhance their safety, and the safety of all road users, while addressing their mobility needs and quality of life.

# Older Drivers at Work
## Key points
People 55 years and older are a growing group of the U.S. population that continues to work and drive. While older workers are more likely to adopt safe driving behaviors, they are also at greater risk of serious injury if they are involved in a crash. Employers can take actions to keep older drivers safe on the job.
texts.3:
# Older Drivers at Work
## Why it's important
Older workers (those ages 55 and older) bring extensive skills, knowledge, and experience built over the course of a lifespan. However, age-related physical and mental changes may affect older workers’ driving. While such changes are normal, they also put older drivers at a greater risk of dying if they are in a motor vehicle crash. Employers and workers share the responsibility for keeping older drivers safe at work.
texts.4:
# Older Drivers at Work
## Facts and stats
*   By 2030, 32% of the U.S. population is expected to be age 55 or older, an increase from 30% in 2022. The share that is age 65 or older will grow even more: from 17% in 2022 to 21% in 2030.1  
*   Over the 2016-2026 period, workers ages 75 and older are expected to have the fastest rate of growth in the labor force (91.5%), followed by workers 65 to 74 years (50.3%).2  
*   By 2030, 85% to 90% of Americans age 65 or older will be licensed to drive.3  
*   Research shows that older drivers are more likely than their younger counterparts to adopt safe behaviors such as wearing a seat belt and complying with speed limits. However, those age 55 and older have twice the risk of dying in a work-related crash than younger workers do.4 It is normal for physical and mental abilities to decline with age – putting older workers at greater risk of serious injury if they are involved in a motor vehicle crash.  
*   In 2022 motor vehicle crashes accounted for 36% of all work-related deaths among workers age 55 or older.5
texts.5:
# Older Drivers at Work
## What employers can do
Use the following recommendations to develop safety and health programs that consider older drivers' needs.
*   Consider whether the work can be done without driving. Reducing the amount of driving workers do is the most effective way to prevent motor vehicle crashes.  
*   Set policies that allow drivers to consult with their supervisors to adjust driving hours if they have trouble seeing at night, and to stop driving if they are too tired or the weather is bad.  
*   Provide refresher driving training that includes topics such as safe-driving strategies, changes in road rules, regulations on distracted driving, and new vehicle safety features.  
*   Restrict driving based on assessment of actual driving ability, rather than general health status or an arbitrary age limit.  
*   Give workers general information about the possible effects of prescription and over-the-counter medications on their driving.
texts.6:
# Older Drivers at Work
## What workers can do
If you are an older worker driving as part of your job:
*   Talk with your doctor or pharmacist about potential effects of your medications on safe driving.  
*   Get a thorough eye exam at least every 1-2 years, as your vision may change with age.  
*   Maintain good health by engaging in regular physical activity, eating a healthy diet, getting enough sleep, and complying with all health exams and screenings.  
*   Use a driving self-assessment tool to evaluate your driving.  
*   Talk with your supervisor if you are having difficulty with driving, as you may need to change your driving habits.

# Older Drivers
## Overview
In 2021 more than 20% of licensed drivers in the United States were 65 or older (FHWA, 2022). As drivers age, their physical and mental abilities, driving behaviors, and crash risks all change, though age alone does not determine driving performance. Many features of the current system of roads, traffic signals and controls, laws, licensing practices, and vehicles were not designed to accommodate older drivers. Older Americans are increasingly dependent on driving to maintain their mobility, independence, and health. The challenge is to balance mobility for older drivers with safety for all road users.
The U.S. population 65 and older increased at a much faster rate (35.1%) than the total population (7.4%) from the years 2010 to 2020 (U.S. Census Bureau, 2010, 2020). The U.S. Census Bureau estimates that by 2030 the resident population over 65 will be 73 million and will comprise 21% of the total U.S. population (Vespa et al., 2020).
As the U.S. population 65 and older has grown, the proportion of licensed drivers 65+ has also risen, from 14% in 2001 to 21% in 2021 (FHWA, 2002, 2022). The proportion of fatal crashes involving older drivers follows a similar trend, rising from 11% in 2001 to 19% in 2021.

# Older Drivers
## Overview
_*Projected numbers based on 2017 population estimates_
_Sources: FHWA (2002, 2022); NCSA (2012); Stewart (2023); U. S. Census Bureau (2011, 2021); Vespa et al. (2020)_
The number of fatalities involving older drivers has been increasing in recent years, after experiencing a period of decline from 2000 to 2009. In 2021 there were 8,209 fatalities involving older drivers compared to the 29-year low of 5,613 in 2009 (NCSA, 2012; NHTSA, 2023). However, the older population has grown at a rate faster than the increase in fatalities involving older drivers.

# Older Drivers
## Overview
Not only is the U.S. population aging, with older people making up a larger proportion of the total population, but drivers are maintaining their licenses for longer as well. The proportion of people 65 or older who held driver licenses rose from 78% in 2001 to 89% in 2021 (FHWA, 2002,2022b; U.S. Census Bureau 2011, 2022). Notably, 59% of people 85 years and older maintained their licenses in 2020, compared to approximately half (50%) who maintained licenses in 2000 (FHWA, 2002, 2022b).
With current life expectancy in this country at 78.8 years on average (Kochaneck et al., 2020), and with advances in medical science, older Americans are staying mobile and active longer. Those who will reach 65 in the coming decade have been projected to drive more miles and are expected to continue driving later in life than previous generations. This increasingly active and mobile older population gives rise to the need to enhance their safety, and the safety of all road users, while addressing their mobility needs and quality of life.
